chapter: Zulu, Nice and the Punch Miller incident
title: Armstrong's feelings about New Orleans and segregation
summary: He loved the city, felt no victim of segregation there, and had blocked out his early days.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Okay. And at that time he swore he'd never come back here again, because he was mad at the city. He held the jazz club responsible for all that.
Well, yeah, what was generally his feelings about New Orleans overall?

Well, you know, in earlier times when I was with him when he was talking to somebody else about New Orleans, and he would always introduce me as being from New Orleans, he generally had a warm attitude about it, that there's no other place like it, you know, the food is fabulous, and as far as he was concerned the climate was perfect and all that. And he saw it in a kind of a rosy glow. Right. And as far as the segregation and all that was concerned, well he just assumed that that was the way it was going to be, since it was in the south and all that. But it didn't bother him in the first place. In the first place he never really felt like a victim of it.
You believe that Louie never felt that he was a victim of segregation?

Yeah, never felt like he was a victim of segregation. Not in New Orleans, although he felt it frequently outside of New Orleans. Anyway, but he was at home here, you know, he knew a lot of people and people treated him well. His early days here, he pretty much had blocked out of his mind, although he remembered certain individuals. Such as? Well he remembered Peter Davis and he remembered Jones and he remembered Stella Oliver, certainly. He remembered him.
